title: How Automatic Doors Know When Someone Is Standing in Front of Them
excerpt: Automatic doors do not recognise you. Sensors report a change, a controller decides, and a motor does the moving.
imageAlt: Illustration for How Automatic Doors Know When Someone Is Standing in Front of Them
content:
Automatic doors open so smoothly that people rarely stop to think about what makes them work. Walk toward the entrance of a supermarket, airport, or office building, and the doors slide apart before you touch them. Once you pass through, they close again.

But how does the door know someone is approaching? It does not recognize people the way a human does. Instead, it uses sensors to detect movement, changes in distance, or the presence of an object within a specific area.

Motion Sensors Detect Someone Approaching

Many automatic sliding doors use microwave motion sensors. These devices send out high-frequency radio waves toward the area in front of the entrance.

When a person walks through this area, the waves reflect back differently. The sensor detects the change and sends a signal to the door's control system.

This process is based on the Doppler effect, a principle also used in radar technology. When an object moves toward or away from a sensor, the frequency of the reflected waves changes slightly. The sensor can use this change to identify movement.

Once movement is detected in the correct area, the controller activates the door-opening mechanism.

Some Doors Use Infrared Sensors Instead

Not every automatic door depends on movement detection. Some use infrared technology to identify people or objects near the entrance.

Active infrared sensors emit invisible infrared light and measure the light reflected from nearby objects. When someone enters the detection area, the reflected signal changes, allowing the system to recognize that something is present.

Passive infrared sensors work differently. They detect changes in infrared energy, which is naturally emitted by warm objects, including the human body.

These technologies are useful in different situations. A motion sensor may detect someone walking toward a door, while a presence sensor can help keep the door open when someone is standing in its path.

The Door's Controller Decides When to Open

Sensors do not move the doors themselves. They send information to a controller, which decides whether the door should open, remain open, or close.

When the controller receives a valid detection signal, it activates a motor connected to the door's opening mechanism. In sliding doors, this motor moves the panels along a track. In automatic swing doors, it operates an arm or mechanical drive that pushes the door open.

The controller also manages how long the door stays open. Some systems use a fixed opening time, while others keep the door open as long as their sensors continue detecting someone in the doorway.

How Automatic Doors Avoid Closing on People

Opening the door is only half the job. It must also close without hitting someone who is entering or leaving.

To prevent accidents, automatic doors often have safety sensors that monitor the doorway and nearby areas. These may use infrared beams, presence detection, or other sensing methods.

If a person remains in the doorway, the system can delay closing. Some doors also stop or reverse their movement if an obstruction is detected while they are closing.

This is why automatic doors sometimes stay open longer than expected. The system may be detecting someone who is still passing through, even if they are not directly in front of the entrance.

Why Some Automatic Doors Open Without Anyone Nearby

You may have seen an automatic door open when nobody appears to be standing in front of it. This can happen because its sensor detects movement outside the area you can easily see.

A microwave sensor may respond to movement farther away from the entrance. Reflections, nearby moving objects, or poorly adjusted detection zones can also trigger the system.

In busy locations, sensors are configured to balance convenience with safety. If the detection area is too small, people may have to walk very close before the door opens. If it is too large, the door may open unnecessarily.

A Simple System Working in the Background

Automatic doors combine sensors, electronic controllers, motors, and safety mechanisms to operate without human assistance.

The sensors detect movement or presence, the controller decides what should happen, and the motor moves the door. Additional safety devices help prevent it from closing while someone is passing through.

The next time an automatic door opens as you approach, remember that it is not recognizing you personally. It is responding to changes detected by sensors and following instructions from a small control system.

faq.q: What sensors do automatic doors use?
faq.a: Most use microwave motion sensors or infrared sensors, and often both a motion sensor and a separate safety sensor.

faq.q: Why does a door sometimes open when nobody is there?
faq.a: The sensor can pick up movement outside the area you can see, or its detection zone may be set too wide.

faq.q: How do automatic doors avoid closing on people?
faq.a: Safety sensors watch the doorway. If something is in the way, the door waits, stops or reverses.

note: Sensing, deciding and moving are three separate jobs. Keeping them apart is what makes automatic doors both smooth and safe.
